thread.title: US mortgage debt reaches $13.17 trillion with rising delinquency and foreclosure rates
thread.title_full: US mortgage debt reaches $13.17 trillion with rising delinquency and foreclosure rates

author: k. t. goins
title: US mortgage debt reaches $13.17 trillion with rising delinquency and foreclosure rates
text:
Americans owed $13.17 trillion in mortgage debt as of the fourth quarter of 2025, making up 70.1% of total U.S. consumer debt, according to a Mar. 26 report from LendingTree based on Federal Reserve Bank of New York data.
This level of debt underscores the central role that mortgages play in household finances across the country, while also highlighting trends in loan performance such as delinquency and foreclosure rates.
The number of active mortgage accounts rose to 86.94 million by late 2025, with an average balance per account reaching $151,484—up from $118,075 in late 2019. The increase reflects both rising home prices and continued borrowing activity over recent years.
Serious delinquency rates have climbed as well: In Q4 2025, just under one percent (0.92%) of all U.S. mortgage balances were at least 90 days past due—a figure that has risen each year since Q4 2022 when it stood at only 0.43%. Despite this uptick, mortgages remain among the most stable forms of consumer debt; for comparison, serious credit card delinquencies reached much higher levels at nearly thirteen percent during the same period.
Foreclosure activity also saw a notable rise in the last year: In 2025 there were approximately 227,360 new foreclosures nationwide—a jump from about 174,100 recorded in the previous year and marking a thirty percent increase year-over-year. However, even with this growth in foreclosures compared to recent years’ lows following pandemic-era protections and economic shifts—the total remains significantly below historical highs such as those seen in mid-2010s when annual new foreclosures exceeded four hundred thousand.
These figures suggest that while overall mortgage health remains relatively strong compared to other types of consumer borrowing—and despite recent increases—serious distress levels are still far lower than those observed ten years ago.
